rich_summary: Vyasa urges Yudhishthira to begin the Ashvamedha (Horse‑sacrifice), assuring him that the immense gifts of gold and the proper performance of the rite will cleanse the sin of killing his kinsmen in the war. The king undertakes the ritual with exact adherence to Vedic prescriptions. Priests conduct complex ceremonies—Pravargya, Soma rites, and the preparation of numerous sacrificial stakes—while Bhima distributes endless food so that no visitor is poor or hungry. Animals, including the wandering sacrificial horse, are consecrated and offered. Draupadi participates in the culminating rite, and Yudhishthira symbolically inhales the purifying smoke. When the sacrifice ends, the king gives vast wealth to the Brahmanas and even donates the entire Earth to Vyasa, declaring his willingness to renounce it, astonishing the assembly.

highlight_spans.why: Vyasa’s opening command marks the formal beginning of Yudhishthira’s Ashvamedha and frames the chapter’s central ritual.
The urgency of the moment emphasizes the sacred timing and inevitability of the king’s atoning sacrifice.

top_scenes.scene_text: The vast Ashvamedha arena filled with priests, golden stakes, and a Garuda-shaped altar while crowds watch and Bhima oversees endless distribution of food.
Draupadi seated solemnly beside the divided sacrificial horse as priests conduct the final rites and smoke rises from the sacred fire.
Yudhishthira presenting the entire Earth as a gift to Vyasa before astonished kings and Brahmanas at the conclusion of the sacrifice.
